analysis: Independent read-only colour-distribution and cross-run identity analysis of Writing device text

method.crop: Unrotated laptop question only, from its recorded DOM bounds, excluding the tablet overlap by ending 5px before its recorded left edge. Crop coordinates are [left, top, right-exclusive, bottom-exclusive].
method.backgroundVerification: The uniform background is the most common RGB value in every analysed crop. The foreground is the exact recorded computed question colour in every case.
method.coverageFormula: For channel c, a_c = (B_c - P_c) / (B_c - F_c), where B is background, F is text foreground and P is the screenshot pixel. Coverage spread = max(a_R,a_G,a_B) - min(a_R,a_G,a_B).
method.edgeSelection: Keep pixels whose mean channel coverage is strictly between 0.05 and 0.95. This excludes clear background and near-solid foreground.
method.interpretation: A scalar grayscale coverage blend lies close to one RGB line and therefore has nearly equal per-channel coverage, allowing integer rounding. Large channel spreads and complementary coloured fringes demonstrate separate channel coverage, consistent with LCD/subpixel antialiasing.
method.diagnosticBoundary: The 0.05 spread marker classifies this pixel distribution; it is not a changed checkpoint tolerance and is not used to pass a screenshot comparison.
method.imageHandling: Images were read only. Crops exist in memory for numerical analysis. No saved PNG was edited, padded, resampled or substituted.

findings: At 1440 in the third run, published laptop question edges have scalar coverage (maximum channel spread about 0.00721), whereas 98.35% of source edge pixels have channel spread above 0.05. At 901 the pattern reverses: 98.25% of published edge pixels exceed 0.05, and no source edge pixel does.

All twelve 1280/1440 laptop question crops across the three runs resolve to exactly two raw RGB byte identities: one scalar/grayscale-like variant and one channel-separated/LCD-like variant. The crop text and layout are identical, and the variant is not bound to published or source.

The unchanged protected 1280 screenshot is byte-identical between runs one and three, but uses the grayscale-like question variant in run two. Published 1440 uses the LCD-like variant in runs one and two and grayscale-like in run three.

Source 768 and source 1440 full PNGs are each byte-identical between runs one and three; their question rasterisation is grayscale-like in run two. Source commits differ, so these exact screenshot identities do not prove all source files were unchanged.

Every third-run fixed sample set is byte-identical at planned times 0, 250 and 750ms. For 1440 the elapsed samples span 122–854ms published and 125–869ms source. The observed difference persists over this capture window; another short settling delay is not justified by these data.

At the unchanged pixel-channel threshold 24, all 25,296 changed pixels in the 1440 failing pair and all 16,200 changed pixels in the 901 failing pair lie within the device bands; none lie in the heading or practice-action bands.
inference: These results strongly support different text antialiasing/rasterisation states as a concrete component of the Writing difference. The unchanged protected implementation varies between the two states across runs, so the evidence does not support a simple fixed source-only typography mismatch. A stable compositing/raster state influenced by earlier rendering history is compatible with the observations.
notEstablished: Pixel analysis does not identify the responsible compositor layer, compositing reason or browser event.
The inherited 0.001ms reduced-motion transform transition and initial scale 0.97 remain a causal hypothesis. No transition was disabled or changed in this analysis.
The laptop question analysis does not prove that every changed device pixel is explained exclusively by text antialiasing; layer rasterisation can also affect borders and other content.
The existing Writing screenshot failures remain failures. These diagnostics do not relax thresholds or grant rendered acceptance.
